title: De Morgan's laws with a universal set
statements: (A B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ. ∪
(A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ Bᶜ. ∪
tactical_explanations:
**A) (A B)ᶜ = {9, 10}. ∪**  (true)

A B = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}; taking the complement relative to U leaves exactly {9,10}. ∪

**B) (A B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ. ∪**  (true)

This is De Morgan's law for sets, and it holds generally — the complement of a union equals the intersection of the complements.

**C) (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ Bᶜ. ∪**  (true)

This is the other De Morgan's law — the complement of an intersection equals the union of the complements — and it also holds generally.

**D) A ∩ B = {4, 5, 6}.**  (false)

A ∩ B consists of elements in both sets: only 4 and 5 qualify (6 is in B but not in A), so A ∩ B = {4,5}, not {4,5,6}.

**E) (A ∩ B)ᶜ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10}.**  (false)

Since A ∩ B = {4,5}, its complement relative to U is everything else: {1,2,3,6,7,8,9,10}. The set given here wrongly includes 4 and 5 and wrongly omits 6, 7, and 8.
solution_overview:
Let U = {1, 2, ..., 10} be the universal set, A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, and B = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}.

**Part 1: Setup.**

Compute once: A B = {1,...,8}, so (A B)ᶜ = {9,10}; A ∩ B = {4,5} (only elements in both), ∪ ∪ so (A ∩ B)ᶜ = {1,2,3,6,7,8,9,10}. Both De Morgan identities, (A B)ᶜ=Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ and (A ∩ B)ᶜ=Aᶜ Bᶜ, hold generally and ∪ ∪ can be checked against these two computed values.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (TRUE) (A B)ᶜ = {9, 10}. ∪

**2.** (TRUE) (A B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ. ∪

**3.** (TRUE) (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ Bᶜ. ∪

**4.** (FALSE) A ∩ B = {4, 5, 6}.

**5.** (FALSE) (A ∩ B)ᶜ = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10}.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

title: Cartesian products
context: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y, z}.
statements: A × B = B × A.
The number of elements in B × A equals the number of elements in A × B.
tactical_explanations:
**A) |A × B| = 6.**  (true)

The Cartesian product A × B has |A| × |B| = 2 × 3 = 6 ordered pairs.

**B) (2, x) A × B. ∈**  (true)

2 A and x B, so the ordered pair (2,x), with first coordinate from A and second from B, belongs to ∈ ∈ A × B.

**C) (x, 2) A × B. ∈**  (false)

In A × B, the first coordinate must come from A. Since x A, the pair (x,2) does not belong to A × B. ∉

**D) A × B = B × A.**  (false)

A × B contains pairs like (2,x) where the first entry is from A; B × A would need its first entry from B, so e.g. (2,x) B × A since 2 B. The two products contain different pairs in general. ∉ ∉

**E) The number of elements in B × A equals the number of elements in A × B.**  (true)

Even though the pairs themselves differ, both products contain |A| × |B| = |B| × |A| = 6 elements — the counts match even when the sets of pairs don't.
solution_overview:
Let A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y, z}.

**Part 1: Setup.**

|A×B| = |A|·|B| = 2·3 = 6 in both directions, but the pairs themselves differ: A×B always has its FIRST coordinate from A, while B×A has its first coordinate from B — so (2,x) A×B but (x,2) A×B, and A×B ∈ ∉ ≠ B×A as sets of pairs even though |A×B| = |B×A|.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (TRUE) |A × B| = 6.

**2.** (TRUE) (2, x) A × B. ∈

**3.** (FALSE) (x, 2) A × B. ∈

**4.** (FALSE) A × B = B × A.

**5.** (TRUE) The number of elements in B × A equals the number of elements in A × B.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

title: Sets defined by inequalities
context: Let A = {x R : 1 ∈ < x < 5} and B = {x R : x ≥ 3}.
statements: A B. ⊆
A ∩ B = {x R : 3 ≤ x < 5}, i.e. the interval [3, 5). ∈
B A. ⊆
A ∪ B = {x R : x > 1}, i.e. the interval (1, ∞). ∪ ∈
There exists a real number that belongs to A but not to B.
tactical_explanations:
**A) A B. ⊆**  (false)

A contains values like x = 2, which satisfies 1 < 2 < 5 but not 2 ≥ 3, so x = 2 A but x = 2 B — this ∈ ∉ counterexample shows A is not a subset of B.

**B) A ∩ B = {x R : 3 ≤ x < 5}, i.e. the interval [3, 5). ∈**  (true)

Combining both conditions (1 < x < 5 and x ≥ 3), the binding restrictions become 3 ≤ x < 5, exactly the interval [3,5).

**C) B A. ⊆**  (false)

B contains values like x = 10, which is not less than 5, so x = 10 B but x = 10 A — B is not a ∈ ∉ subset of A.

**D) A ∪ B = {x R : x > 1}, i.e. the interval (1, ∞). ∪ ∈**  (true)

A covers (1,5) and B covers [3,∞); together every value greater than 1 is covered by one set or the other, with no gaps, giving exactly (1,∞).

**E) There exists a real number that belongs to A but not to B.**  (true)

x = 2 satisfies 1 < 2 < 5 (so x A) but does not satisfy x ≥ 3 (so x B). ∈ ∉
solution_overview:
Let A = {x R : 1 ∈ < x < 5} and B = {x R : x ≥ 3}.

**Part 1: Setup.**

A = (1,5) and B = [3,∞) as intervals. Overlap them once: A ∩ B = [3,5) (the tighter bound wins on each side), and A B = (1,∞) (no gap between the two, since A already reaches past 3). Neither interval contains the ∪ other — x=2 is in A but not B, and x=10 is in B but not A.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (FALSE) A B. ⊆

**2.** (TRUE) A ∩ B = {x R : 3 ≤ x < 5}, i.e. the interval [3, 5). ∈

**3.** (FALSE) B A. ⊆

**4.** (TRUE) A ∪ B = {x R : x > 1}, i.e. the interval (1, ∞). ∪ ∈

**5.** (TRUE) There exists a real number that belongs to A but not to B.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

title: Symmetric difference
statements: The symmetric difference can also be written as AΔB = (A \ B) ∩ (B \ A).
A ∩ B AΔB. ⊆

tactical_explanations:
**B) The symmetric difference can also be written as AΔB = (A \ B) ∩ (B \ A).**  (false)

A \ B and B \ A are always disjoint from each other (one requires being outside B, the other requires being inside B), so their intersection is always empty — this can never equal the actual (generally nonempty) symmetric difference, and the correct connective is , not ∩ . ∪

**C) A ∩ B AΔB. ⊆**  (false)

A ∩ B = {3,4}, which by definition is exactly what symmetric difference excludes (it only keeps elements in exactly one set) — so A ∩ B and AΔB are disjoint here, not one contained in the other.

**D) If A and B are disjoint, then AΔB = A B. ∪**  (true)

If A ∩ B = , then A \ B = A and B \ A = B, so AΔB = A B. ∅ ∪

**E) |AΔB| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|.**  (true)

Here |A|=4, |B|=4, |A ∩ B|=2, giving 4+4−2(2)=4, matching |{1,2,5,6}|=4 — and this identity holds in general.
solution_overview:
Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6}.

**Part 1: Setup.**

A\B={1,2} and B\A={5,6}, so AΔB = {1,2} {5,6} = {1,2,5,6}, with |AΔB|=4. Since A\B and ∪ B\A are always disjoint from each other, their UNION (not intersection) is the correct formula; and since A ∩ B={3,4} is exactly what AΔB excludes, the two are always disjoint from one another too.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**3.** (FALSE) A ∩ B AΔB. ⊆

**4.** (TRUE) If A and B are disjoint, then AΔB = A B. ∪

**5.** (TRUE) |AΔB| = |A| + |B| − 2|A ∩ B|.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

title: Frost protection and irrigation
context: Let A = {T R : T² ∈ < 16} be the set of temperatures (in °C) for which grapevines are considered frost-safe, and let B = {T R : T ≥ −1} be the set of temperatures at which ∈ the irrigation system is switched on. Note that A is the open interval (−4, 4) and B is the closed-below interval [−1, ∞).
statements: 4 is an element of A ∩ B.
The complement of A in R is {T R : T < −4 or T > 4}. ∈
A B is equal to the entire set of real numbers R. ∪
There exists a temperature that is frost-safe (in A) but does not trigger irrigation (not in B).
tactical_explanations:
**A) A ∩ B = [−1, 4).**  (true)

A ∩ B needs T ≥ −1 (from B) and −4 < T < 4 (from A); combining these, the binding constraints are T ≥ −1 and T < 4, giving exactly [−1, 4).

**B) 4 is an element of A ∩ B.**  (false)

T = 4 gives T² = 16, which is not strictly less than 16, so 4 is not in A — and therefore not in A ∩ B either.

**C) The complement of A in R is {T R : T < −4 or T > 4}. ∈**  (false)

Trap: since A = (−4, 4) is an OPEN interval, it excludes both boundary points −4 and 4 — so both must belong to the complement. The correct complement is {T : T ≤ −4 or T ≥ 4} (using ≤ and ≥), not the strict version with < and > shown here, which wrongly leaves the two boundary points out of the complement too.

**D) A B is equal to the entire set of real numbers R. ∪**  (false)

A B = (−4, ∞): every point covered by A or B is greater than −4, and no point ≤ −4 belongs to ∪ either set. For example, T = −10 is in neither A nor B, so the union is not all of R.

**E) There exists a temperature that is frost-safe (in A) but does not trigger irrigation (not in B).**  (true)

Take T = −2: T² = 4 < 16, so −2 A (frost-safe), but −2 ≥ −1 is false, so −2 B (irrigation off). This ∈ ∉ is a valid temperature in A but not in B.
solution_overview:
Let A = {T R : T² ∈ < 16} be the set of temperatures (in °C) for which grapevines are considered frost-safe, and let B = {T R : T ≥ −1} be the set of temperatures at which ∈ the irrigation system is switched on. Note that A is the open interval (−4, 4) and B is the closed-below interval [−1, ∞).

**Part 1: Setup.**

A=(−4,4) (open) and B=[−1,∞) (closed at −1). Overlap: A ∩ B=[−1,4) (B's lower bound and A's upper bound both bind); union: A B=(−4,∞) (no gap, since A already reaches down past −1). Because A is open, ∪ its complement must include both boundary points: Aᶜ={T≤−4 or T≥4}.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (TRUE) A ∩ B = [−1, 4).

**2.** (FALSE) 4 is an element of A ∩ B.

**3.** (FALSE) The complement of A in R is {T R : T < −4 or T > 4}. ∈

**4.** (FALSE) A B is equal to the entire set of real numbers R. ∪

**5.** (TRUE) There exists a temperature that is frost-safe (in A) but does not trigger irrigation (not in B).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

title: Customer survey overlap
context: Let A be the set of customers who like Product A, with |A| = 120. Let B be the set of customers who like Product B, with |B| = 90. It is found that |A ∩ B| = 50 customers like both products.
statements: The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170. ∪
The number of customers who like neither product is 40.
The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.
A ∩ B A. ⊆
Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170. ∪**  (false)

Trap: by inclusion–exclusion, |A B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| = 120 + 90 − 50 = 160, not 170 — a ∪ simple arithmetic slip.

**B) The number of customers who like neither product is 40.**  (true)

Out of 200 surveyed customers, 160 like at least one product (part a), so 200 − 160 = 40 like neither.

**C) The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.**  (false)

Trap: customers who like only Product A are those in A but excluded from the overlap: |A| − |A ∩ B| = 120 − 50 = 70, not 90.

**D) A ∩ B A. ⊆**  (true)

Every customer who likes both products necessarily likes Product A, so by definition the intersection is always a subset of A (and, symmetrically, of B) — this holds for any two sets, not just this survey.

**E) Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.**  (false)

Trap: this only forces |A ∩ B| ≥ |A| + |B| − 200 = 210 − 200 = 10, a MINIMUM bound, not an exact value. The actual overlap (50, as given) is consistent with, and comfortably exceeds, this minimum — "exactly 10" overreaches what the bound alone can prove. PART II — Logic Tier 1 — Foundations
solution_overview:
Let A be the set of customers who like Product A, with |A| = 120. Let B be the set of customers who like Product B, with |B| = 90. It is found that |A ∩ B| = 50 customers like both products.

**Part 1: Setup.**

By inclusion–exclusion: |A B| = |A|+|B|−|A ∩ B| = 120+90−50 = 160, so 200−160=40 like ∪ neither, and |A only| = |A|−|A ∩ B| = 120−50=70. Separately, since |A B|≤200 always, the counts 120+90=210 alone ∪ force |A ∩ B|≥210−200=10 as a guaranteed minimum — the actual value 50 comfortably exceeds this floor.

**Part 2: Check each claim.**

**1.** (FALSE) The number of customers who like at least one of the two products, |A B|, is 170. ∪

**2.** (TRUE) The number of customers who like neither product is 40.

**3.** (FALSE) The number of customers who like only Product A (A but not B) is 90.

**4.** (TRUE) A ∩ B A. ⊆

**5.** (FALSE) Since |A| + |B| = 210 exceeds the 200 customers surveyed, this proves that EXACTLY 10 customers like both products, with no other value being possible.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
